Turning a 2D boundary into a circle (a 1D cyclic order)
Points in the order they appear around the square
The distance named in the question
Can we choose `k` points with every pair at least `d` apart?
Try each point as the first chosen point
The circle has no natural starting point
From the last chosen point, move forward to the first point at least `d` away
Greedy: take the nearest valid next point

binary search on `d` between `0` and `2 * side`

head: lo, hi

`ok(mid)`
Reason
rows: from `(0,0)` the greedy picks `(2,0)`, `(2,2)` leave only `(1,2)`, at distance 1; every other start also stops at 3 points
`(0,0)`, `(2,0)`, `(2,1)`, `(2,2)` are pairwise at least 1 apart, and the wrap-around distance is 4

blocks.h: Why does greedy work for a fixed start?
p: Once the first point is fixed, taking the nearest point that is at least `d` away leaves the largest possible set of points for the later choices. Trying every point as the start covers the cyclic wrap-around.

bullets: Time: O(n^2 · log side), because each start moves forward through at most `n` points, and the binary search takes about log(2·side) steps.

3464.takeaway: Order the points around the perimeter, binary search the distance, and test it greedily from every starting point while checking the wrap-around.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Indices sorted by `nums1`, so all smaller values come first
A min-heap holding the `k` largest `nums2` values seen so far, and their sum
Finds the group of equal `nums1` values
Ties must not see each other
Assign the answer to every index in the group before adding any of them
Keep only the `k` largest by evicting the smallest

blocks.h: Why assign the group before pushing?
p: The values in a group have equal `nums1`, and the question needs strictly smaller. Giving all members the sum from before the group guarantees none of them uses another member of the same group.

3478.takeaway: Sort by nums1 and sweep with a size-k min-heap of nums2 values, giving each group of equal keys the sum from before the group.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: `pos = {x for x in nums if x > 0}`
Keeping one copy of each value
Sum of all distinct positive values
The best possible subarray after deleting
Keep just the single largest element

p: Because we may delete elements first, we can delete every duplicate, zero and negative number, leaving the distinct positive values as one array of unique elements, whose whole sum is the answer.

blocks.h: Why is the no-positives case different?
p: If there is no positive number, any subarray with more than one element can only get smaller or equal, so the best is a single element: the largest one. Zero is counted as "not positive" here, which is fine because the maximum would then be 0 itself.

3487.takeaway: Delete everything except one copy of each positive value; if none is positive, the answer is the maximum element.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Splits the string into maximal runs of equal characters
Working with runs instead of single characters
Only runs that have a neighbour on both sides can be traded
A run of 1s must be surrounded by 0s
This run is a block of 1s

The zero runs on its two sides: after the trade they and the block form one run of zeros bounded by 1s, which can all be turned into 1s. The block's own 1s are lost and regained, so the net gain is the two zero runs
Computing the net gain of a trade

p: The string already has two 1s, plus the best gain 5, giving `7`. For `"0100"` the only 1-run has neighbours of lengths 1 and 2, giving `1 + 3 = 4`.

blocks.h: Why does a trade gain exactly the two neighbouring zero runs?
p: First the 1-block becomes zeros, so the left zeros, the block and the right zeros form one long zero run. That run is bounded by 1s (the original ones next to it, or the imaginary 1 padded at either end of the string), so it can be turned entirely into 1s. The block's own cells end up as 1 again, so the net change in the number of 1s is the left run plus the right run.

3499.takeaway: Split into runs; trading a 1-run that sits between two zero runs gains the lengths of those two zero runs, so take the best such run.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: True when the gap between neighbours in the sorted array is too wide to jump
Detecting a break in a sorted sequence
Component number of node `i`: it increases by 1 at every wide gap
Two nodes are connected exactly when they are in the same group

p: With `comp = [0,1,1,1]` the queries `(0,1)`, `(0,2)`, `(1,3)`, `(2,3)` give `[False, False, True, True]`.

Because the array is sorted, if a gap between two neighbouring values is larger than `maxDiff`, then any pair of values on opposite sides is even farther apart, so no edge crosses the gap. If every neighbouring gap is small, the nodes form a chain. Hence each connected component is a block of consecutive indices.

3532.takeaway: In a sorted array the components are blocks separated by gaps larger than maxDiff, so label them and compare labels.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: A monotonic stack (increasing from bottom to top) of the distinct positive levels currently "open"
Tracking the heights seen to the left
A smaller value ends the larger levels: they were handled by earlier operations and cannot continue past `x`
Zeros need no operation, and they have already cleared everything above them from the stack
`if not st or st[-1] < x:` push and `ops += 1`
A new, higher level appears that no open operation covers, so it needs its own operation
The same value is already open, and the earlier operation can also cover this occurrence

blocks.h: Why does an equal value on the stack cost nothing?
p: If the same value is on the stack with nothing smaller between the two occurrences, one operation on the whole subarray between them zeroes both. Smaller values in between would have popped it. So the second occurrence is covered by the first operation.

bullets: Time: O(n), each element is pushed and popped at most once.

3542.takeaway: A monotonic stack counts the distinct levels that need their own operation; equal levels with nothing smaller between them share one.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Fills `depth[v]` (distance from the root) and `up[0][v]` (the parent)
The `2^j`-th ancestor of `v`, built by `up[j][v] = up[j-1][up[j-1][v]]`
The lowest common ancestor (LCA): lift the deeper node to the same depth, then lift both together from the largest jump down
Number of edges on the path from `u` to `v`
Ways to give `d` edges weights 1 or 2 so that the sum is odd: half of all `2^d` assignments

blocks.h: Why is it exactly half of the assignments?
p: The sum is odd exactly when an odd number of the edges carry weight 1. Among the `2^d` assignments of 1 or 2, those with an odd number of 1s are half of them, which is `2^(d−1)` when `d ≥ 1`. With no edges the sum is 0 (even), so the answer is 0.

bullets: Space: O(n log n) for the jump table.

3559.takeaway: Answer each query with the path length d from an LCA computation: 2^(d−1) odd assignments (and 0 when d is 0).

The middle element itself belongs to neither side
With `x` as the middle value: ways to choose a left partner and a right partner both equal to `2x`
Fix the middle element and multiply
Move the current element to the "left" side

p: A triplet is determined by its middle index `j`; the left and right partners are then chosen independently from the earlier and later elements equal to `2 · nums[j]`. Multiplying the two counts and summing over all `j` counts every triplet exactly once.

3583.takeaway: Fix the middle index; multiply the counts of 2·x on its left and on its right.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Topological order of the DAG (Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take nodes with no remaining incoming edges)
Shortest paths on a DAG in one pass
Is there a valid path using only edges of cost at least `s` whose total cost is at most `k`?
Feasibility test for the binary search on the score
Cheapest total cost to reach `u` using allowed edges
DP (dynamic programming) over the topological order
`if dist[u] == INF or (u != 0 and u != n - 1 and not online[u])` skip
Unreachable or offline nodes cannot be passed through
`if c >= s and dist[u] + c < dist[v]`
Only edges of cost at least `s` are allowed, and we relax the cost
The cheapest valid path fits the budget
If a path with all edges at least `s` exists, one also exists for any smaller `s`, so search for the largest `s`

blocks.h: Why does the score become a threshold?
p: The score of a path is its smallest edge cost, so "score at least `s`" means every edge on the path costs at least `s`. Restricting the graph to such edges turns the score into a yes/no question, and the DAG shortest path then tests the cost limit `k`.

bullets: Time: O((n + m) log C), where C is the largest edge cost.

3620.takeaway: Binary search the minimum edge cost; for each guess compute the cheapest path over a topological order using only edges at or above the guess.

Best sum of "increase, then decrease" ending at `i`
Best sum of the full "increase, decrease, increase" shape ending at `i`
Going up: extend `inc1` (or start it from `nums[i−1]`), and extend `inc2` or start it after a decreasing part
The two phases that go up
Going down: extend `dec` or start it after the first increasing run
Nothing is updated, which resets all three phases at this index (they stay `−∞`)
A flat step breaks any strict shape
The best complete shape ending anywhere

p: The answer is `14`, the whole array `1, 4, 2, 7`.

blocks.h: Why can the phases share an element?
p: In the required shape the turning points belong to two neighbouring phases (the peak ends the increase and starts the decrease). The DP (dynamic programming) handles this by starting the next phase from the previous index's value, so the turning element is counted once in the sum.

3640.takeaway: A three-state DP (up, down, up again) along the array, where equal neighbours break the shape.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Only the relative order of values matters, so use ranks inside `[l, r]`
Counting patterns over an ordered range
Number of valid arrays so far that end with value `v` after an upward step
Number that end with value `v` after a downward step
Arrays of length 2: the previous value is any smaller (`v` choices) or any larger (`size − 1 − v` choices)
`new_up[v] = sum of down[u] for u < v`
After a down step, the next must be up to a larger value
`new_down[v] = sum of up[u] for u > v`
After an up step, the next must be down to a smaller value
Prefix sums (from the left for `up`, from the right for `down`) make each layer O(size) instead of O(size²)

p: Now `sum(up) + sum(down) = 1 + 1 = 2`, matching the arrays `[4,5,4]` and `[5,4,5]`.

blocks.h: Why do only the last value and direction matter?
p: The next element must go in the opposite direction from the last step and cannot equal the last value. So all that decides what can follow is the last value and whether the last step was up or down.

3699.takeaway: Track, for each last value, the number of arrays whose last step was up or down, and alternate using prefix sums.

Stack (runs)

the remaining pairs are added the same way

blocks.h: Why store runs and not single characters?
p: A k-balanced substring is defined by runs of exactly `k` parentheses of each kind. With counts stored per run, checking and deleting `k` characters is O(1) instead of scanning back `2k` positions.

3703.takeaway: Keep a stack of (character, run length); when a run of ) reaches length k right after at least k opening brackets, delete the k + k characters.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Prefix sums of `+1` for each `target` and `−1` for any other value
Turning a counting condition into a sum
In the subarray `i .. j−1` the number of targets exceeds the number of non-targets, i.e. `target` is a strict majority
A positive sum means the majority
Check every pair of prefix positions

blocks.h: Why does "sum greater than 0" mean "more than half"?
p: If the subarray has `t` targets and `o` other elements, its sum is `t − o`. It is positive exactly when `t > o`, which is the same as `2t > t + o`, the length of the subarray.

3737.takeaway: Map elements to +1/−1 and count the pairs of prefix sums that increase.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: `+1` for a good node, `−1` for a bad one
An order in which each node appears before its children (from a stack-based traversal) and each node's parent, with root `0`
Best score of a connected group that contains `u` and lies inside `u`'s subtree: `val[u]` plus the positive `down` values of its children
Add a child's contribution only when it is positive
Best score of a group containing `u` in the whole tree
Start from `u`'s subtree, and add what the parent side can give: the parent's best group without the branch through `u`

p: `full[p]` already includes the best contribution of the branch through `u`, which is `max(0, down[u])`. To know what the parent side can offer to `u` we must remove that branch, otherwise it would be counted twice.

3772.takeaway: Compute the best subtree group bottom-up, then reroot top-down, removing a child's own contribution when passing the parent's value down.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Numbers from `1000` to `n`; each of them has one comma (up to `n = 10^5`, written `100,000`)
Counting by ranges of digit length
If `n < 1000` there are no commas at all

p: Commas appear first in `1,000`. With the limit `n ≤ 10^5`, no number has more than one comma.

blocks.h: Why only one comma per number?
p: A second comma would appear only from `1,000,000`, which is beyond the limit of `10^5`. For larger limits you would add one more for every number from `10^6`, and so on.

3870.takeaway: Every number from 1000 upward (up to 10^5) has exactly one comma, so the count is max(0, n − 999).

Cyclic rotation with the modulo operator
The grid after all row rotations

Element that lands at row `i` of column `j` after the column is rotated upward by `colShift[j]`
Wraps the index around the end

blocks.h: Why compute rows first and then columns?
p: The two steps do not commute in general, so the order matters. Building `rows` first and then reading from it for the column step gives exactly "all rows first, then all columns".

4052.takeaway: Rotate every row with modular indexing, then rotate every column of the result the same way.
